title: What can you say about hyaluronic acid in your ads and on your site?
summary: The library gives no supported wording for hyaluronic acid, because no listed source supports one at a dose. Avoid wording that names or implies a disease, a drug or a treatment, such as "Relieves osteoarthritis or arthritis knee pain".

wordings_to_avoid.wording: Relieves osteoarthritis or arthritis knee pain
wordings_to_avoid.why: Names a disease; FDA's 2000 rule (page 1016) treats joint pain as characteristic of arthritis.

evidence_gap: No listed source gives a use or dose for oral hyaluronic acid. Health Canada's monograph list (checked 2026-10-14) has no monograph for it, no ODS fact sheet among those read covers it, FDA's lists show no health claim for it, and Regulation (EU) No 432/2012 has no claim for it. Until a listed source covers it, the library supports no wording for it.

evidence_strengths.strong: At least two listed sources support it independently at a comparable dose and form, and none disagrees.
evidence_strengths.moderate: One listed source supports it as an evidence-based use at that dose, and no listed source disagrees.
evidence_strengths.limited: The only support is traditional use, the sources disagree, or the source itself calls the evidence weak.

reasons_to_avoid.drug: names a drug or presents the product as one
reasons_to_avoid.treatment: promises to treat, cure or prevent a condition

disclaimer: Not legal advice. This guide shows the wording that published evidence supports at a daily dose, from the sources linked below; it is not a ruling on any claim. Your own product, its form and dose, and your own evidence still need to match the wording you use.
